title: Part 1, Chapter 15
paragraphs: In which is related the unfortunate adventure that Don Quixote fell into when he fell out with certain heartless Yanguesans

The sage Cid Hamete Benengeli relates that as soon as Don Quixote had taken leave of his hosts and all who had been present at the burial of Chrysostom, he and his squire rode into the same wood that they had seen the shepherdess Marcela enter. After wandering through it in all directions for more than two hours in search of her without finding her, they came to a halt in a glade covered with tender grass, beside which ran a pleasant cool stream that invited and indeed compelled them to spend there the hours of midday heat, which by now was coming on heavily. Don Quixote and Sancho dismounted, and turning Rocinante and the ass loose to graze on the abundant grass, they rummaged in the saddlebags, and without any ceremony, very peacefully and sociably, master and man made their meal of what they found in them.

Sancho had not thought it worth hobbling Rocinante, sure from what he knew of the horse's staidness and chastity that all the mares in the Cordova pastures would not lead him into anything improper. Chance, however, and the devil — who is not always asleep — arranged it so that grazing in this very valley was a drove of Galician ponies belonging to some Yanguesan carriers, whose habit it was to take their midday rest with their teams in places where grass and water were plentiful; and the spot Don Quixote happened to choose suited the Yanguesans' purpose very well. So it happened that Rocinante took a fancy to amuse himself with these ponies, and dropping his usual gait and demeanour as soon as he caught their scent, he, without asking his master's leave, broke into a brisk little trot and hurried over to make his wishes known to them. They, however, evidently preferring their pasture to him, received him with their heels and teeth so effectively that they soon broke his girths and left him naked, without a saddle to cover him. Worse still, the carriers, seeing the violence he was offering their mares, came running up armed with stakes and beat him so thoroughly that they brought him to the ground sorely battered.
By this time Don Quixote and Sancho, who had watched the drubbing of Rocinante, came up panting, and Don Quixote said to Sancho:

"So far as I can see, friend Sancho, these are not knights but low-born people of mean birth: I mention it because you can lawfully help me to take proper vengeance for the insult offered to Rocinante before our eyes."
"What the devil vengeance can we take," Sancho answered, "when they are more than twenty and we are not more than two — or, indeed, perhaps not more than one and a half?"

"I count for a hundred," replied Don Quixote, and without another word he drew his sword and attacked the Yanguesans; and excited and impelled by his master's example, Sancho did the same. To begin with, Don Quixote delivered a slash at one of them that laid open the leather jerkin he wore, together with a great portion of his shoulder. The Yanguesans, seeing themselves attacked by only two men while they were so many, fell to their stakes, and driving the pair into the middle of them, began to lay on with great zeal and energy. In fact, at the second blow they brought Sancho to the ground, and Don Quixote fared no better, despite all his skill and high spirit; and fate would have it that he should fall at the feet of Rocinante, who had not yet risen — proof of how furiously stakes can pound in angry boorish hands.
Then, seeing the damage they had done, the Yanguesans with all possible haste loaded their team and continued on their way, leaving the two adventurers a sorry sight and in a sorrier mood.
Sancho was the first to come round, and finding himself close to his master he called to him in a weak and doleful voice, "Señor Don Quixote, ah, Señor Don Quixote!"
"What is it, brother Sancho?" Don Quixote answered in the same feeble, suffering tone as Sancho.

"I'd like, if it were possible," replied Sancho Panza, "for your worship to give me a couple of sips of that fiery Blas potion of yours, if you have any of it to hand; perhaps it will be as good for broken bones as it is for wounds."

"If I only had it here, wretch that I am, what more could we want?" said Don Quixote. "But I swear to you, Sancho Panza, on the faith of a knight-errant, that before two days are out, unless fortune decides otherwise, I mean to have it in my possession, or my hand will have lost its cunning."
"But in how many days does your worship think we shall have the use of our feet again?" answered Sancho Panza.

"As for myself, I cannot guess how many," said the battered knight Don Quixote; "but I take all the blame on myself, for I had no business drawing my sword against men who were not dubbed knights like me. I believe that as a punishment for breaking the laws of chivalry, the God of battles has allowed this chastisement to be administered to me. For that reason, brother Sancho, you should take note of what I am about to tell you, since it matters greatly to the welfare of both of us. When you see rabble of this sort offering us insult, you are not to wait for me to draw my sword against them, for I shall not do it at all; you draw your sword and punish them to your heart's content, and if any knights come to their aid and defence I will take care to defend you and attack them with all my might. You have already seen by a thousand signs and proofs what the might of this strong arm of mine is equal to" — so puffed up had the poor gentleman become by his victory over the stout Biscayan.

But Sancho did not approve of his master's instruction enough to let it pass without reply: "Señor, I am a man of peace, meek and quiet, and I can put up with any affront because I have a wife and children to support and bring up. So let it be a hint to your worship — since it cannot be a command — that on no account will I draw a sword either against peasant or against knight, and that here before God I forgive any insults that have been, are, or shall be offered me, by high or low, rich or poor, noble or commoner, no rank or condition whatever excepted."

To all of which his master replied, "I wish I had breath enough to speak a little more easily, and that the pain I feel in my side would ease enough to let me explain to you, Panza, the mistake you are making. Come now, sinner, suppose the wind of fortune, so far so adverse, should turn in our favour, filling the sails of our desires so that safely and without obstacle we put into port at one of those islands I have promised you — how would it be with you if, having won it, I made you lord of it? Why, you would make that almost impossible by not being a knight, and not wanting to be one, and not having the courage or the will to avenge insults or defend your lordship. For you must know that in newly conquered kingdoms and provinces the minds of the inhabitants are never so settled, nor so well-disposed to their new lord, that there is no fear of their stirring up another change to try, as they say, what chance may bring them. So it is essential that the new possessor have good sense enough to govern, and valour enough to attack and defend himself, whatever may happen."

"In what has just happened to us," answered Sancho, "I'd have been glad to have that good sense and that valour your worship speaks of. But I swear, on the faith of a poor man, that I am more fit for plasters than for arguments. See if your worship can get up, and let us help Rocinante, though he doesn't deserve it, since he was the main cause of all this thrashing. I never would have thought it of Rocinante — I took him for as virtuous a person and as quiet as myself. They are right when they say that it takes a long time to get to know people, and that nothing is sure in this life. Who would have said that, after such mighty slashes as your worship gave that unlucky knight-errant, there was coming, riding post and right at their heels, such a great storm of sticks as has fallen on our shoulders?"

"And yet yours, Sancho," Don Quixote replied, "ought to be used to such squalls. But mine, raised in soft cloth and fine linen, plainly must feel the pain of this mishap more keenly. And if I did not imagine — why do I say imagine? — know for certain that all these annoyances are very necessary parts of the calling of arms, I would lie down here and die of pure vexation."

To this the squire replied, "Señor, since these mishaps are the harvest one reaps from chivalry, tell me — do they happen very often, or do they have their own fixed times for coming round? Because it seems to me that after two such harvests we shall be no good for a third, unless God in his infinite mercy helps us."

"Know, friend Sancho," answered Don Quixote, "that the life of knights-errant is subject to a thousand dangers and reverses, and is no less within the immediate possibility of becoming kings and emperors, as experience has shown in the case of many different knights whose histories I know well. I could tell you now, if the pain would let me, of some who simply by the might of their arm rose to the high stations I have mentioned; and those same knights, both before and after, suffered various misfortunes and miseries. The valiant Amadis of Gaul found himself in the power of his mortal enemy Arcalaus the magician, who, it is positively claimed, while holding him captive gave him more than two hundred lashes with the reins of his own horse while he was tied to one of the pillars of a courtyard. And there is a certain little-known author of no small authority who says that the Knight of Phoebus, caught in a pitfall that opened under his feet in a certain castle, on falling found himself bound hand and foot in a deep pit underground, where they administered to him one of those things they call clysters, of sand and snow-water, that nearly finished him; and if he had not been rescued in that grim extremity by a sage who was a great friend of his, it would have gone very hard with the poor knight. So I can well suffer in the company of such worthy folk, for the indignities they had to suffer were greater than what we are suffering. For I want you to know, Sancho, that wounds caused by any instruments that happen by chance to be in hand inflict no indignity, and this is laid down in the law of the duel in express terms: if, for instance, a cobbler strikes another with the last he holds in his hand, although it is in fact a piece of wood, it cannot for that reason be said that the man he struck has been cudgelled. I say this so you don't imagine that because we have been drubbed in this affair we have therefore suffered any indignity, for the weapons those men carried, and pounded us with, were nothing more than their stakes, and not one of them, so far as I remember, carried rapier, sword, or dagger."

"They gave me no time to see all that much," answered Sancho, "for hardly had I laid hand on my _tizona_ when they signed the cross on my shoulders with their sticks in such style that they took the sight out of my eyes and the strength out of my feet, stretching me out where I now lie. And the question whether or not those stake-strokes were an indignity gives me no trouble, but the pain of the blows does; they'll remain as deeply imprinted on my memory as on my shoulders."
"For all that, let me tell you, brother Panza," said Don Quixote, "that there is no memory time does not put an end to, and no pain death does not remove."

"And what greater misfortune can there be," replied Panza, "than the kind that waits for time to put an end to it and death to remove it? If our mishap were one of those that are cured with a couple of plasters, it wouldn't be so bad; but I am beginning to think that all the plasters in a hospital would scarcely be enough to put us right."

"No more of that: draw strength out of weakness, Sancho, as I mean to do," returned Don Quixote, "and let us see how Rocinante is, for it seems to me that not the smallest share of this mishap has fallen to the poor beast."
"There is nothing strange in that," replied Sancho, "since he too is a knight-errant; what I do wonder at is that my donkey should have come off scot-free where we come out scotched."

"Fortune always leaves a door open in adversity, to bring relief to it," said Don Quixote; "I say so because this little beast may now make up for the lack of Rocinante, carrying me from here to some castle where I can be cured of my wounds. And I shall not count it any dishonour to be so mounted, for I remember having read how the good old Silenus, tutor and instructor of the merry god of laughter, when he entered the city of the hundred gates, rode very contentedly on a handsome ass."
"It may be true that he rode mounted as your worship says," answered Sancho, "but there is a great difference between riding mounted and being slung across like a sack of manure."

To which Don Quixote replied, "Wounds received in battle confer honour rather than take it away; so, friend Panza, say no more about it, but, as I told you before, get up as well as you can and put me on top of your beast in whatever fashion you like, and let us go from here before night comes and surprises us in these wilds."
"And yet I have heard your worship say," observed Panza, "that it is quite proper for knights-errant to sleep in wastes and deserts, and that they consider it very good fortune."

"That," said Don Quixote, "is when they cannot help it, or when they are in love. And so true is this that there have been knights who stayed two years on rocks, in sunshine and shade and all the inclemencies of heaven, without their ladies knowing anything about it. One of these was Amadis, when, under the name of Beltenebros, he settled on the Peña Pobre for — I don't know whether it was eight years or eight months, for I am not sure of the count; in any case he stayed there doing penance for some quarrel the Princess Oriana had with him. But no more of this now, Sancho, and make haste before some mishap like Rocinante's befalls the ass too."

"The very devil would be in it then," said Sancho. And letting off thirty "ohs" and sixty sighs and a hundred and twenty curses and execrations on whoever it was that had brought him there, he raised himself, stopping halfway bent like a Turkish bow, unable to bring himself fully upright; and with all his pains he saddled his ass, which had also strayed somewhat, yielding to the excessive licence of the day. He then raised up Rocinante, who, if he had had a tongue to complain with, would assuredly have outdone both Sancho and his master in lamentation.

To be brief: Sancho fixed Don Quixote on the ass and tied Rocinante along with a leading rein, and taking the ass by the halter, he proceeded more or less in the direction in which it seemed to him the high road might be. As chance was now conducting their affairs from good to better, he had not gone a short league when the road came in sight, and on it he spotted an inn, which, to his annoyance and to Don Quixote's delight, must necessarily be a castle. Sancho insisted it was an inn, his master that it was not — that it was a castle — and the dispute lasted so long that before it was settled they had reached the place. And so Sancho entered with all his team without any further argument.
